claim: Salmonella enterica comprises more than 2000 non-typhoidal and typhoidal serovars inducing a variety of conditions ranging from benign gastroenteritis to severe systemic infection.
source: Salmonella enterica, a Gram-negative facultative intracellular pathogen, comprises more than 2000 non-typhoidal and typhoidal serovars inducing a variety of conditions ranging from benign gastroenteritis to severe systemic infection (Gogoi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gogoi et al., 2019, which provides external scholarly support for the statement.

claim: Every year typhoidal serovars infect 20 millions of people and cause more than 200,000 of deaths.
source: Every year typhoidal serovars infect 20 millions of people and cause more than 200,000 of deaths (Crump et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Crump et al., 2004, providing external evidence for the epidemiological data.

claim: In some cases, Salmonella establishes a chronic infection that results in asymptomatic carriers hosting the environmental reservoir for further infections.
source: In some cases, Salmonella establishes a chronic infection that results in asymptomatic carriers hosting the environmental reservoir for further infections (Monack, 2012; Ruby et al., 2012; Gal-Mor, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Monack, 2012; Ruby et al., 2012; Gal-Mor, 2019, providing external scholarly support.

claim: Salmonella resides within the draining lymph nodes and systemic tissues such as the spleen, where the bacteria survive mainly inside macrophages.
source: Salmonella resides within the draining lymph nodes and systemic tissues such as the spleen, where the bacteria survive mainly inside macrophages and have to deal with this hostile environment (Eisele et al., 2013; Garai et al., 2012; Ehrhardt et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eisele et al., 2013; Garai et al., 2012; Ehrhardt et al., 2023, providing external scholarly support.

claim: Salmonella can replicate within macrophages inside modified vacuoles called phagosomes and escape the host's defenses.
source: Capitalizing on different virulence factors, Salmonella can replicate within macrophages inside modified vacuoles called phagosomes and escape the host's defenses (LaRock et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to LaRock et al., 2015, providing external scholarly support.

claim: Salmonella uses strategies to interfere with macrophage polarization.
source: In addition, as reported for several intracellular bacterial pathogens, Salmonella uses strategies to interfere with macrophage polarization (Thiriot et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thiriot et al., 2020, providing external scholarly support.

claim: Macrophages form a continuum of activation states whose two extremes are the pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages that have a bactericidal activity, and the anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages that promote the resolution of inflammation and healing.
source: In vivo, they form a continuum of activation states whose two extremes are the pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages, that have a bactericidal activity, and the anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages that promote the resolution of inflammation and healing (Ginhoux et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ginhoux et al., 2016, providing external scholarly support.

claim: During the first hours of infection, most bacteria, including Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium, induce macrophage polarization toward the pro-inflammatory and microbicidal M1 phenotype.
source: During the first hours of infection, most bacteria, including Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (S. Typhimurium), induce macrophage polarization toward the pro-inflammatory and microbicidal M1 phenotype (Jenner and Young, 2005; Nau et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jenner and Young, 2005; Nau et al., 2002, providing external scholarly support.

claim: Persisting bacteria, like Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Brucella abortus, or S. Typhimurium, may preferentially reside inside healing/anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages.
source: In contrast, persisting bacteria, like Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Brucella abortus, or S. Typhimurium, may preferentially reside inside healing/anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages (Eisele et al., 2013; Thiriot et al., 2020; Xavier et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eisele et al., 2013; Thiriot et al., 2020; Xavier et al., 2013, providing external scholarly support.

claim: In a mouse model of S. Typhimurium long-term infection, bacteria were shown to persist mainly in M2 macrophages.
source: In a mouse model of S. Typhimurium long-term infection, bacteria were shown to persist mainly in M2 macrophages (Eisele et al., 2013; Pham et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eisele et al., 2013; Pham et al., 2020, providing external scholarly support.

claim: S. Typhimurium reside in inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS)-expressing macrophages that clustered within splenic granulomas 42 days post-infection in mice.
source: In contrast, another in vivo study showed that S. Typhimurium reside in inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS)-expressing macrophages that clustered within splenic granulomas 42 days post-infection in mice (Goldberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Goldberg et al., 2018, providing external scholarly support.

claim: Intracellular replication of S. Typhimurium was shown to vary according to macrophage polarization, with a greater replication in M2 macrophages.
source: In addition, intracellular replication of S. Typhimurium was shown to vary according to macrophage polarization, with a greater replication in M2 macrophages (Saliba et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Saliba et al., 2016, providing external scholarly support.

claim: The transparent zebrafish embryo has emerged as a powerful vertebrate model to study host–pathogen interactions at the cellular and whole organism level.
source: Perfectly suited to live observation of immune cells and pathogens in vivo, the transparent zebrafish embryo has emerged as a powerful vertebrate model to study host–pathogen interactions at the cellular and whole organism level (Torraca and Mostowy, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Torraca and Mostowy, 2018, providing external scholarly support.

claim: Macrophages first express pro-inflammatory cytokines (M1-like polarization) before switching to a new state expressing both M1 and M2 makers during the wound healing process in a non-infected wound model.
source: Using a non-infected wound model, we previously showed that macrophages first express pro-inflammatory cytokines (M1-like polarization) before switching to a new state expressing both M1 and M2 makers during the wound healing process (Nguyen-Chi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nguyen-Chi et al., 2015, providing external scholarly support for the authors' previous work.

claim: When less than 500 colony-forming units (CFU) of Sal-GFP were injected, all zebrafish larvae survived the infection.
source: When less than 500 colony-forming units (CFU) of Sal-GFP were injected, all zebrafish larvae survived the infection (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C showing survival curves.

claim: HBV injection of 1000–2000 CFU of Sal-GFP led to 50% of larvae survival at 4 dpi.
source: On the other hand, HBV injection of 1000–2000 CFU of Sal-GFP led to 50% of larvae survival at 4 dpi (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1D showing survival curves.

claim: After injecting 1000–2000 CFU, bacteria efficiently proliferated in 47% of infected larvae, from 1 to 4 dpi.
source: After injecting 1000–2000 CFU, bacteria efficiently proliferated in 47% of infected larvae, from 1 to 4 dpi (50,000–200,000 CFU, Figure 1E, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1E and 1G showing CFU counts and infection outcomes.

claim: Among the 53% of infected larvae that survived the infection at 4 dpi, 40% harbored live bacteria (10–2000 CFU), while 36% were bacteria free.
source: Among the 53% of infected larvae that survived the infection at 4 dpi, 40% harbored live bacteria (10–2000 CFU), while 36% were bacteria free (Figure 1E, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1E and 1G showing CFU counts and infection outcomes.

claim: Alive infected larvae still harbored persistent bacteria at 14 dpi.
source: Importantly, alive infected larvae still harbored persistent bacteria at 14 dpi (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C showing CFU counts at 14 dpi.

claim: At 3 hpi, infected larvae showed elevated levels of expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines: interleukin-1 beta (il-1b), tumor necrosis factor a and b (tnfa and tnfb), interleukin-8 (il-8), and of the inflammation marker matrix metalloproteinase 9 (mmp9).
source: At 3 hpi, infected larvae showed elevated levels of expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines: interleukin-1 beta (il-1b), tumor necrosis factor a and b (tnfa and tnfb, two orthologs of mammalian TNF), interleukin-8 (il-8), and of the inflammation marker matrix metalloproteinase 9 (mmp9) (Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 2A showing gene expression levels.

claim: Pro-inflammatory gene expression (il-1b, tnfb, il-8, and mmp9) significantly decreased at 1 dpi and raised from 2 hpi to 4 dpi to reach similar levels to those detected at 3 hpi.
source: Subsequently, pro-inflammatory gene expression (il-1b, tnfb, il-8, and mmp9) significantly decreased at 1 dpi and raised from 2 hpi to 4 dpi to reach similar levels to those detected at 3 hpi.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing temporal changes in gene expression.

claim: Salmonella infection induced ccl38a.4 gene, encoding CCL2, a key chemokine of macrophage migration that binds the CCR2 receptor at 4 hpi.
source: Salmonella infection induced ccl38a.4 gene, encoding CCL2, a key chemokine of macrophage migration that binds the CCR2 receptor (Cambier et al., 2014) at 4 hpi but has no effect on cxcr4b and sdf1 (cxcl12a), suggesting a role of the Ccl2/Ccr2 axis in macrophage mobilization to the infection site (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and a citation to Cambier et al., 2014.

claim: The up-regulation of the macrophage-specific marker mfap4 during the time course of infection highlighted an overall macrophage response.
source: The up-regulation of the macrophage-specific marker mfap4 during the time course of infection highlighted an overall macrophage response (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 2A showing mfap4 expression.

claim: The macrophage-specific marker mpeg1 was down-regulated early after Salmonella infection.
source: In contrast, we found that the other frequently used macrophage-specific marker mpeg1 was down-regulated early after Salmonella infection (Figure 2A), as previously described during Salmonella and Mycobacterium marinum infections in zebrafish (Benard et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2A and a citation to Benard et al., 2015.

claim: Salmonella infection led to an increase in the global macrophage population that persisted over days compared to PBS-injected larvae.
source: We noticed that Salmonella infection led to an increase in the global macrophage population that persisted over days compared to PBS-injected larvae, suggesting that Salmonella infection triggers myelopoiesis (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data in Figures 3A and 3B showing macrophage numbers over time.

claim: At 3 hpi macrophages were specifically recruited to the HBV of infected embryos.
source: At 3 hpi macrophages were specifically recruited to the HBV of infected embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing macrophage localization.

claim: At 4 dpi, an intense macrophage accumulation persisted in the brain of infected embryos.
source: In addition, at 4 dpi, an intense macrophage accumulation persisted in the brain of infected embryos, in line with the development of a Salmonella persistent localized infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing macrophage accumulation at 4 dpi.

claim: Macrophage depletion increased larval mortality up to 54% at 4 dpi while control group showed 4% mortality after infection with a sublethal dose of 500 CFU of Sal-GFP.
source: After infection with a sublethal dose of 500 CFU of Sal-GFP, MTZ-mediated macrophage depletion increased larval mortality up to 54% at 4 dpi while control group showed 4% mortality (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F showing survival curves after macrophage depletion.

claim: MTZ-mediated macrophage depletion strongly impacted bacterial clearance with development of a systemic infection.
source: MTZ-mediated macrophage depletion also strongly impacted bacterial clearance with development of a systemic infection, as shown by fluorescence microscopy and quantification of bacterial burden (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G, H showing bacterial burden.

claim: Both macrophages and neutrophils were strongly recruited to the infection site in the first hours of infection compared to controls.
source: Total volume analysis showed that macrophages and neutrophils were both strongly recruited to the infection site in the first hours of infection compared to controls and that their mobilization slightly diminished over time post-infection with similar kinetics (Figure 3G, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data in Figures 3G and 3H showing leukocyte recruitment.

claim: Infected larvae displayed a massive accumulation of macrophages in the HBV, with clusters associated with persisting fluorescent Salmonella at 4 dpi.
source: Infected larvae displayed a massive accumulation of macrophages in the HBV, with clusters associated with persisting fluorescent Salmonella (Figure 4A, shown with arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 4A showing macrophage clusters with bacteria at 4 dpi.

claim: Salmonella resided mainly inside some macrophages and only few Salmonella outside macrophages were observed at 4 dpi.
source: 3D reconstruction of mfap4-positive cell volumes from confocal images revealed that Salmonella resided mainly inside some macrophages and only few Salmonella outside macrophages were observed (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D reconstruction data in Figure 4B showing bacterial localization.

claim: Few neutrophils were present in the HBV at 4 dpi, but they were not clustered and did not contain persistent Salmonella.
source: Similar experiments with neutrophil reporter embryos, Tg(mpx:GFP), showed that although persisting bacteria could be observed, few neutrophils were present in the HBV at 4 dpi, but they were not clustered and did not contain persistent Salmonella (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figures 4C and 4D showing neutrophil distribution and bacterial localization at 4 dpi.

claim: Macrophage recruitment was five time stronger at 4 dpi than at 16 hpi.
source: Quantification of the total volume of recruited macrophages (mfap4+ cells) and neutrophils (mpx+ cells) in HBV confirmed an important macrophage recruitment, which was five time stronger at 4 dpi than at 16 hpi (Figures 3H and 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data comparing macrophage volumes at different time points in Figures 3H and 4F.

claim: The frequencies of infected macrophages within the recruited macrophage population ranged from 20% to 30% in the early stages to around 60% during the late stages (4 dpi).
source: Moreover, we quantified the proportion of macrophages harboring bacteria, revealing that the frequencies of infected macrophages within the recruited macrophage population ranged from 20% to 30% in the early stages to around 60% during the late stages (4 dpi) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5A showing the percentage of infected macrophages over time.

claim: During the first hours of infection, a maximum of 80% of mfap4-positive cells became also tnfa-positive (mfap4+tnfa+ cells) corresponding to M1-like activated macrophages.
source: During the first hours of infection, a maximum of 80% of mfap4-positive cells became also tnfa-positive (mfap4+tnfa+ cells) corresponding to M1-like activated macrophages (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 6B showing the percentage of M1 macrophages.

claim: Both macrophages with and without bacteria expressed tnfa during early infection.
source: Interestingly, both macrophages with and without bacteria expressed tnfa (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6C showing tnfa expression in infected and bystander macrophages.

claim: The vast majority of accumulated macrophages at 4 dpi were tnfa-negative (less than 10% were tnfa-positive).
source: Macrophage volume analysis revealed that few tnfa-positive macrophages (mfap4+tnfa+ cells) were still present at the infection site (less than 10%), but that the vast majority of accumulated macrophages were tnfa-negative (Figure 6D–F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data in Figures 6D-F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C showing tnfa expression at 4 dpi.

claim: Persistent Salmonella were found within tnfa-negative macrophages at late stages of infection.
source: In agreement with the finding that the vast majority of accumulated macrophages at 4 dpi were not expressing tnfa, persistent Salmonella were found within tnfa-negative macrophages at late stages of infection (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6E showing bacterial localization in tnfa-negative macrophages.

claim: A large majority of mfap4+ cells (mCherry+) were tnfa− (GFP−) both at 4 hpi and 4 dpi (100% and 90.4% ± 4, respectively) in non-infected condition.
source: FACS analysis on whole larvae in Non-INF condition revealed that a large majority of mfap4+ cells (mCherry+) were tnfa− (GFP−) both at 4 hpi and 4 dpi (100% and 90.4% ± 4, respectively) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 showing cell populations.

claim: The majority (92.5% ± 6) of mfap4+ cells (mCherry+) were tnfa+ (GFP+) at 4 hpi in Sal-INF condition.
source: FACS analysis in Sal-INF condition at 4 hpi revealed that the majority (92.5% ± 6) of mfap4+ cells (mCherry+) were tnfa+ (GFP+), while the majority (80.9% ± 4) were tnfa− (GFP−) at 4 dpi (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 showing cell populations.

claim: The majority (80.9% ± 4) of mfap4+ cells were tnfa− (GFP−) at 4 dpi in Sal-INF condition.
source: FACS analysis in Sal-INF condition at 4 hpi revealed that the majority (92.5% ± 6) of mfap4+ cells (mCherry+) were tnfa+ (GFP+), while the majority (80.9% ± 4) were tnfa− (GFP−) at 4 dpi (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 showing cell populations.

claim: Salmonella infection induced massive changes of gene expression in macrophages at 4 hpi with 3173 up-regulated and 2847 down-regulated genes.
source: Salmonella infection induced massive changes of gene expression in macrophages at 4 hpi (Figure 7D, Figure 7—source data 1) and M1-activated macrophages harbored specific gene expression signature with 3173 up-regulated and 2847 down-regulated genes
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 7D and Figure 7—source data 1 showing differentially expressed genes.

claim: At 4 dpi, only 104 up-regulated and 440 down-regulated genes were specific to the non-M1 signature.
source: whereas at 4 dpi, only 104 up-regulated and 440 down-regulated genes were specific to the non-M1 signature (Figure 7E, F and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figures 7E, F and Figure 7—source data 1 showing differentially expressed genes.

claim: At 4 hpi, M1-activated macrophages were characterized by a specific up-regulation of pro-inflammatory genes including those involved in the TNF pathway, pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemotaxis, complement, innate immune sensing of pathogens and antimicrobial responses, and matrix metalloproteinases.
source: At 4 hpi, M1-activated macrophages were characterized by a specific up-regulation of pro-inflammatory genes including those involved in the TNF pathway (tnfa, traf4b, traf7, traf1b, tnfrsf1b, tnfrsf9b, tnfaip2, and tnfaip3), pro-inflammatory cytokines (il12a and il12bb), chemotaxis (ccl38a.5, ccl38a.4, ccl19, cxcl18b, and cxcl20), complement (c3a.1, c3a.3, c3a.4, and c3a.6), innate immune sensing of pathogens and antimicrobial responses (tlr5, stat1a, stat2, mxc, irf9, crfb17, card11, card9, and hif1ab), and matrix metalloproteinases (mmp9, mmp14a, mmp14b, mmp11b, mmp13b, mmp30, and mmp23bb) (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing specific gene expression patterns at 4 hpi.

claim: Known markers of M2 and anti-inflammation such as mrc1b, tgm2l, tgfbr2, klf2, klf4, irf2, and mertka were down-regulated at 4 hpi.
source: Interestingly, il10 and il6, that were described for their dual role during inflammation (Mocellin et al., 2003; Scheller et al., 2011), were also up-regulated, while known markers of M2 and anti-inflammation such as mrc1b, tgm2l, tgfbr2, klf2, klf4, irf2, and mertka were down-regulated.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing gene expression patterns and citations to Mocellin et al., 2003; Scheller et al., 2011.

claim: Non-M1-activated macrophages at 4 dpi specifically up-regulated genes involved in anti-inflammation and M2 markers in mammalian systems.
source: In contrast non-M1-activated macrophages at 4 dpi specifically up-regulated genes involved in anti-inflammation and M2 markers in mammalian systems (c1qtnf6b, cxcl13, dgat1a, cfhl2 [ortholog of F13B in human], phgdh, f5, kmo, and ppp1r14aa), retinoic acid pathway (rdh10a, rdh12, and ugt1a), bacterial defense (npsn, c9, hamp, and nos2b), regeneration (wt1b), tissue protection and development (cx47.1, lta, and ecm1b), and extracellular matrix remodeling (mmp25b) (Figure 7F, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 7F and Figure 7—source data 1 showing gene expression patterns at 4 dpi.

claim: Top ranking GO terms enriched in macrophages at 4 hpi were 'inflammatory response', 'neutrophil migration', 'macrophage migration', and 'defense response to gram negative bacterium'.
source: Top ranking GO terms enriched in macrophages at 4 hpi were 'inflammatory response', 'neutrophil migration', 'macrophage migration', and 'defense response to gram negative bacterium'.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Enriched KEGG pathways at 4 hpi were 'Protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum', 'phagosome', and 'cytokine–cytokine receptor interactions'.
source: Enriched KEGG pathways were 'Protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum', 'phagosome', and 'cytokine–cytokine receptor interactions' (Figure 7G, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data presented in Figure 7G.

claim: The most significantly enriched KEGG pathways at 4 dpi were 'tight junction' and 'cell adhesion'.
source: KEGG pathways analysis performed on DEGs at 4 dpi revealed the absence of a pro-inflammatory signature and that the most significantly enriched pathways were 'tight junction' and 'cell adhesion' (Figure 7G, Figure 7—source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data presented in Figure 7G.

claim: Macrophages did not express wt1b at 4 hr after infection, but they strongly expressed wt1b 4 days after infection.
source: Confocal microscopy analysis showed that, while macrophages did not express wt1b at 4 hr after infection, they strongly expressed wt1b 4 days after infection. Large clusters of wt1b-positive macrophages harboring persistent bacteria were also observed (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 8 showing wt1b expression in macrophages at different time points.

claim: Many genes related to cell adhesion were differentially regulated in Salmonella infection compared to control.
source: Our transcriptomic analysis data revealed that many genes related to cell adhesion were differentially regulated in Salmonella infection compared to control and that this cell-adhesion signature was not the same during acute and persistent infections (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 9A showing differential expression of cell adhesion genes.

claim: Macrophage motility at the injection site was enhanced in infected larvae at 1 hpi, with long-distance migration compared to PBS control.
source: Analysis of macrophage trajectories at the injection site revealed that macrophage motility at 1 hpi was enhanced in infected larvae, with long-distance migration compared to PBS control (Figure 9B and Videos 8, 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by trajectory analysis data in Figure 9B and Videos 8, 9 showing macrophage movement.

claim: Macrophage motility at the injection site at 4 dpi in infected larvae was decreased compared to PBS control, with very short trajectories.
source: In contrast, macrophage motility at the injection site at 4 dpi in infected larvae was decreased compared to PBS control, with very short trajectories.
evidence: This claim is supported by trajectory analysis data showing macrophage movement at 4 dpi.

claim: Macrophage migration speed was significantly enhanced at 1 hpi in the infected larvae compared to the control condition.
source: In addition, macrophage migration speed was significantly enhanced at 1 hpi in the infected larvae compared to the control condition, whereas at 4 dpi, this speed was reduced compared to the control condition (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 9C showing macrophage velocity.

claim: At 4 dpi, macrophage migration speed was reduced compared to the control condition.
source: In addition, macrophage migration speed was significantly enhanced at 1 hpi in the infected larvae compared to the control condition, whereas at 4 dpi, this speed was reduced compared to the control condition (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 9C showing macrophage velocity.

claim: At 1 hpi, bystander macrophages exhibited heightened velocity during acute infection, while infected macrophages maintained a speed comparable to the control group.
source: At 1 hpi, bystander macrophages exhibited heightened velocity during acute infection, while infected macrophages maintained a speed comparable to the control group (Figure 9D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 9D comparing velocities of bystander and infected macrophages.

claim: During persistent infection (4 dpi), both bystander and infected macrophages exhibited reduced velocity compared to unstimulated macrophages.
source: In contrast, during persistent infection (4 dpi), both bystander and infected macrophages exhibited reduced velocity compared to unstimulated macrophages (Figure 9D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 9D comparing velocities of different macrophage populations.

claim: At 1 hpi, neutrophil speed was increased by the infection while at 4 dpi, it was unchanged compared to control.
source: To evaluate the motility of another leukocyte population, we measured neutrophil velocity. At 1 hpi, neutrophil speed was increased by the infection while at 4 dpi, it was unchanged compared to control (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1 showing neutrophil velocity.

claim: Neutrophil velocity was higher than that of macrophages in each condition.
source: Importantly, neutrophil velocity was higher than that of macrophages in each condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of velocity measurements between neutrophils and macrophages.

claim: This study establishes the first larval zebrafish model of S. Typhimurium persistent infection.
source: Here, we establish the first larval zebrafish model of S. Typhimurium persistent infection.
evidence: This claim is stated as a primary finding of the study.

claim: During early stages of infection, both neutrophils and macrophages are mobilized to the infection site to engulf bacteria.
source: Using intravital imaging, we show that during early stages of infection, both neutrophils and macrophages are mobilized to the infection site to engulf bacteria and that macrophages respond by a strong M1-like activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing leukocyte recruitment and phagocytosis.

claim: Macrophages respond by a strong M1-like activation during early stages of infection.
source: Using intravital imaging, we show that during early stages of infection, both neutrophils and macrophages are mobilized to the infection site to engulf bacteria and that macrophages respond by a strong M1-like activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and gene expression data showing M1 polarization.

claim: In later stages of infection, bacteria survive inside non-inflammatory macrophages which accumulate in large clusters.
source: In later stages of infection, bacteria survive inside non-inflammatory macrophages which accumulate in large clusters and provide a niche for persistent bacteria inside the host.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing macrophage clusters with bacteria at late time points.

claim: Non-inflammatory clustered macrophages provide a niche for persistent bacteria inside the host.
source: In later stages of infection, bacteria survive inside non-inflammatory macrophages which accumulate in large clusters and provide a niche for persistent bacteria inside the host.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and transcriptomic data showing bacterial localization in non-inflammatory macrophages.

claim: Transcriptomic profiling of macrophages showed a highly dynamic signature during infection characterized by a switch from pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory/pro-regenerative status.
source: Transcriptomic profiling of macrophages showed a highly dynamic signature during infection characterized by a switch from pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory/pro-regenerative status and revealed a shift in adhesion program.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing temporal changes in gene expression.

claim: Transcriptomic profiling revealed a shift in adhesion program during infection.
source: Transcriptomic profiling of macrophages showed a highly dynamic signature during infection characterized by a switch from pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory/pro-regenerative status and revealed a shift in adhesion program.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing differential expression of adhesion-related genes.

claim: Macrophage trajectory tracking identifies motionless macrophages as a permissive niche for persistent Salmonella.
source: In agreement with this specific adhesion signature, macrophage trajectory tracking identifies motionless macrophages as a permissive niche for persistent Salmonella.
evidence: This claim is supported by trajectory analysis data showing reduced macrophage motility during persistent infection.

claim: Zebrafish model provides a unique platform to explore, in a whole organism, the versatile nature of macrophage functional programs during bacterial acute and persistent infections.
source: Our results demonstrate that zebrafish model provides a unique platform to explore, in a whole organism, the versatile nature of macrophage functional programs during bacterial acute and persistent infections.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Salmonella infection in HBV leads to different outcomes: High Proliferation (systemic infection leading to death), Infected (surviving larvae with persisting bacteria), and Cleared (larvae completely recovered with no more detectable bacteria).
source: Altogether, these results show that Salmonella infection in HBV leads to different outcomes, that we classified as: (1) High Proliferation, indicating a high bacterial burden with systemic infection leading to death; (2) Infected, indicating surviving larvae with persisting bacteria; and (iii) Cleared, indicating that larvae completely recovered with no more detectable bacteria (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by CFU counts, survival data, and imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The outcome of bacterial infections is the result of complex dynamic interactions between the pathogen and the host's cellular and humoral actors of innate immunity.
source: The outcome of bacterial infections is the result of complex dynamic interactions between the pathogen and the host's cellular and humoral actors of innate immunity.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Deciphering the complexity of host-pathogen interactions is necessary to predict infection outcomes and guide therapeutic strategies.
source: Deciphering this complexity is necessary to predict infection outcomes and guide therapeutic strategies.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the importance of understanding host-pathogen interactions.

claim: The development of tractable systems in which bacteria and cellular actors can be tracked at high spatiotemporal resolution in a whole living animal is essential to assess the dynamic of host–pathogen interactions.
source: The development of tractable systems in which bacteria and cellular actors can be tracked at high spatiotemporal resolution in a whole living animal is essential to assess the dynamic of host–pathogen interactions.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the need for appropriate model systems.

claim: The dynamics of interactions between pathogenic bacteria and polarized macrophages between early invasion and late survival remain poorly understood at the organism level.
source: To date, however, the dynamics of interactions between pathogenic bacteria and polarized macrophages between early invasion and late survival remain poorly understood at the organism level.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The dynamics of macrophage polarization in the context of S. Typhimurium infection has not been addressed in zebrafish prior to this study.
source: Yet, the dynamics of macrophage polarization in the context of S. Typhimurium infection has not been addressed in zebrafish.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study.

claim: Previous studies on S. Typhimurium-infected zebrafish larva have been linked to a rapid disease progression with acute symptoms and high production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, leading to larval mortality.
source: Previous studies on S. Typhimurium-infected zebrafish larva, based on intravenous or subcutaneous injection or immersion, have been linked to a rapid disease progression with acute symptoms and high production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, leading to larval mortality (Stockhammer et al., 2009; van der Sar et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stockhammer et al., 2009; van der Sar et al., 2003.

claim: iNOS is a known marker of M1 macrophages.
source: Although iNOS is a known marker of M1 macrophages, the exact polarization status of these macrophages remained undetermined.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about macrophage markers.

claim: The pro-inflammatory cytokine TNFa is a known marker for M1-like macrophage in various species including zebrafish.
source: The pro-inflammatory cytokine TNFa is a known marker for M1-like macrophage in various species including zebrafish (Nguyen-Chi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nguyen-Chi et al., 2015.

claim: Wilms Tumor 1b (wt1b) delineates a pro-regenerative macrophage subset and was shown to be required for heart and fin regeneration in zebrafish.
source: Wilms Tumor 1b (wt1b) delineates a pro-regenerative macrophage subset and was shown to be required for heart and fin regeneration in zebrafish (Sanz-Morejón et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sanz-Morejón et al., 2019.

claim: Cadherins were shown to regulate macrophage functions.
source: Indeed, macrophage function relies on the establishment of contact with neighboring cells and stable attachments to their substrate, allowing transmigration through tissues, positioning, and signaling. Cadherins were shown to regulate macrophage functions (To et al., 2022; Van den Bossche et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to To et al., 2022; Van den Bossche et al., 2015.

claim: Integrins and small GTPases are important for macrophage migration.
source: and integrins and small GTPases are also important for macrophage migration (Aflaki et al., 2011; Paterson and Lämmermann, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aflaki et al., 2011; Paterson and Lämmermann, 2022.

claim: Salmonella persistence was previously associated with M2 macrophages in a mouse model of long-term infection.
source: Salmonella persistence was previously associated with M2 macrophages in a mouse model of long-term infection (Eisele et al., 2013; Goldberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eisele et al., 2013; Goldberg et al., 2018.

claim: M2-permissive macrophage polarization in granulomas is partially dependent on SteE, an effector of the Salmonella pathogenicity island-2 type III secretion system (SPI2 T3SS).
source: Molecularly, M2-permissive macrophage polarization in granulomas is partially dependent on SteE, an effector of the Salmonella pathogenicity island-2 type III secretion system (SPI2 T3SS), while the host cytokine TNF limits M2 polarization (Pham et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pham et al., 2020.

claim: In infected cultured macrophages, SteE regulates STAT3, reorienting macrophage polarization toward M2 phenotypes.
source: In infected cultured macrophages, SteE regulates STAT3, reorienting macrophage polarization toward M2 phenotypes (Gibbs et al., 2020; Panagi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gibbs et al., 2020; Panagi et al., 2020.

claim: Non-growing, antibiotic-tolerant bacteria (persisters) were shown to translocate SPI2 T3SS effectors, including SteE, into the macrophage to reprogram it into a non-inflammatory macrophage.
source: Furthermore, non-growing, antibiotic-tolerant bacteria, also called persisters, were shown to translocate SPI2 T3SS effectors, including SteE, into the macrophage to reprogram it into a non-inflammatory macrophage (Stapels et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stapels et al., 2018.

claim: Mycobacterial granulomas are characterized by epithelioid macrophages expressing tight junction proteins, E-cadherin (CDH1) and ZO-1 (tjp1).
source: Mycobacterial granulomas are characterized by epithelioid macrophages expressing tight junction proteins, E-cadherin (CDH1) and ZO-1 (tjp1) (Cronan et al., 2021; Pagán and Ramakrishnan, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cronan et al., 2021; Pagán and Ramakrishnan, 2018.

claim: In Salmonella-induced granulomas in mice, macrophages weakly express E-cadherin or ZO-1.
source: This is similar to what has been observed in Salmonella-induced granulomas in mice where macrophages weakly express E-cadherin or ZO-1 (Goldberg et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Goldberg et al., 2018.

claim: Salmonella can cause granuloma formation in different animal species including mice and humans.
source: Granulomas are a key pathological feature of some intracellular bacterial infections; they do contain a high proportion of macrophages. Salmonella enterica can cause granuloma formation in different animal species (Work et al., 2019), including mice (Goldberg et al., 2018) and humans (Muniraj et al., 2015; Narechania et al., 2015; Nasrallah and Nassar, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Work et al., 2019; Goldberg et al., 2018; Muniraj et al., 2015; Narechania et al., 2015; Nasrallah and Nassar, 1978.

claim: Ccl2 and its receptor Ccr2 are involved in guiding macrophages toward bacterial pathogens in mice and zebrafish.
source: Previous studies have established the involvement of Ccl2 and its receptor Ccr2 in guiding macrophages toward bacterial pathogens in mice and zebrafish (Cambier et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cambier et al., 2014.

claim: The Salmonella SPI2 T3SS effector SseI, which is involved in long-term infection in mice, has been previously found to modulate the migration of cultured macrophages.
source: Of interest, the Salmonella SPI2 T3SS effector SseI, which is involved in long-term infection in mice, has been previously found to modulate the migration of cultured macrophages (McLaughlin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McLaughlin et al., 2009.

claim: M. marinum uses the ESX-1/RD1 secretion system to enhance macrophage recruitment to nascent granulomas and favor granulomas formation.
source: Subversion of macrophage motility has been also previously observed with another pathogen, M. marinum, which uses the ESX-1/RD1 secretion system to enhance macrophage recruitment to nascent granulomas and favor granulomas formation (Davis and Ramakrishnan, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davis and Ramakrishnan, 2009.

claim: Heterogeneous activity of bacteria creates phenotypically diverse bacterial subpopulations which shape different cellular environments and potentiate adaptation to a new niche in in vitro systems.
source: Indeed, in in vitro systems, heterogeneous activity of the bacteria creates phenotypically diverse bacterial subpopulations which shape different cellular environments and potentiate adaptation to a new niche (Saliba et al., 2016; Avraham et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Saliba et al., 2016; Avraham et al., 2015.

claim: Neutrophils are innate immune players in the defense against Salmonella in various models.
source: Neutrophils are also innate immune players in the defense against Salmonella in various models (Cheminay et al., 2004; Hall et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cheminay et al., 2004; Hall et al., 2012.

claim: Salmonella-induced granulopoiesis has been reported.
source: The fluorescence analysis of global neutrophil populations showed an increase within 2 dpi, in line with the reported Salmonella-induced granulopoiesis (Hall et al., 2012) (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hall et al., 2012.

claim: The initial macrophage response to Salmonella infection was previously shown to be pro-inflammatory in mouse and zebrafish models.
source: The initial macrophage response to Salmonella infection was previously shown to be pro-inflammatory in mouse and zebrafish models (Eisele et al., 2013; Pham et al., 2020; Hall et al., 2013; Ordas et al., 2011; Sheppe et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eisele et al., 2013; Pham et al., 2020; Hall et al., 2013; Ordas et al., 2011; Sheppe et al., 2018.

claim: The activation program detected in human macrophages infected with different pathogens including Salmonella may represent an evolutionarily conserved program for host defense.
source: There are also similarities with the activation program detected in human macrophages infected with different pathogens including Salmonella (Nau et al., 2002), which may represent an evolutionarily conserved program for host defense.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on similarities between zebrafish and human macrophage responses, supported by a citation to Nau et al., 2002.

claim: The internalization of apoptotic RNAs by macrophages during efferocytosis has been demonstrated in the context of murine macrophages co-cultured with apoptotic human T cells.
source: The internalization of apoptotic RNAs by macrophages during efferocytosis has been demonstrated in the context of murine macrophages co-cultured with apoptotic human T cells (Lantz et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lantz et al., 2020.

claim: Macrophages may express genes supporting astrocyte and oligodendrocyte function in the injured microenvironment of the infected HBV.
source: Macrophages may express genes supporting astrocyte and oligodendrocyte function in the injured microenvironment of the infected HBV or these up-regulated genes may reflect the presence of internalized transcripts after efferocytosis in the infected area, as previously observed in other biological context (Lantz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about possible mechanisms, supported by a citation to Lantz et al., 2020.

claim: Up-regulated genes at 4 dpi may reflect the presence of internalized transcripts after efferocytosis in the infected area.
source: Macrophages may express genes supporting astrocyte and oligodendrocyte function in the injured microenvironment of the infected HBV or these up-regulated genes may reflect the presence of internalized transcripts after efferocytosis in the infected area, as previously observed in other biological context (Lantz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about possible mechanisms, supported by a citation to Lantz et al., 2020.

claim: Macrophages participate to the regeneration of axons and the restoration of their function by remyelination and maintenance of myelin homeostasis.
source: In the first scenario, the brain damages caused by the persistent infection may trigger a regenerative response involving pro-regenerative macrophages, which participate to the regeneration of axons and the restoration of their function by remyelination and maintenance of myelin homeostasis (McNamara et al., 2023; Rawji et al., 2016; Tsarouchas et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McNamara et al., 2023; Rawji et al., 2016; Tsarouchas et al., 2018.

claim: The brain damages caused by the persistent infection may trigger a regenerative response involving pro-regenerative macrophages.
source: In the first scenario, the brain damages caused by the persistent infection may trigger a regenerative response involving pro-regenerative macrophages, which participate to the regeneration of axons and the restoration of their function by remyelination and maintenance of myelin homeostasis (McNamara et al., 2023; Rawji et al., 2016; Tsarouchas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about a possible scenario, supported by citations.

claim: During persistent infection, macrophages may perform efferocytosis of damaged or dying cells and internalize transcripts originating from them.
source: Alternatively, during persistent infection, macrophages may perform efferocytosis of damaged or dying cells and internalize transcripts originating from them.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about an alternative scenario.

claim: Both scenarios suggest that the macrophages interact tightly with their microenvironment during persistent infection.
source: Both scenarios suggest that the macrophages interact tightly with their microenvironment during persistent infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the two proposed scenarios.

claim: The dynamic variations in macrophage transcriptomes between acute and persistent infections may indicate disparities in proliferation, death, and polarization, altering the composition of macrophage populations over time.
source: It is important to emphasize that the dynamic variations in macrophage transcriptomes between acute and persistent infections may indicate disparities in proliferation, death, and polarization, altering the composition of macrophage populations over time.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the transcriptomic data.

claim: Dynamic variations in macrophage transcriptomes might denote a phenotypic switch from M1- to M2-like polarization within individual macrophages over time.
source: However, it might also denote a phenotypic switch from M1- to M2-like polarization within individual macrophages over time.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the transcriptomic data.

claim: Non-M1 macrophages which have limited bactericidal activity can be used by Salmonella as a niche to sustain persistent infections in their hosts.
source: Our data indicate that Non-M1 macrophages which have limited bactericidal activity, can be used by Salmonella as a niche to sustain persistent infections in their hosts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the imaging and transcriptomic data showing bacterial localization in non-M1 macrophages.

claim: The host cytokine TNF limits M2 polarization during Salmonella infection.
source: Molecularly, M2-permissive macrophage polarization in granulomas is partially dependent on SteE, an effector of the Salmonella pathogenicity island-2 type III secretion system (SPI2 T3SS), while the host cytokine TNF limits M2 polarization (Pham et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pham et al., 2020.

claim: Motionless macrophages appear non-inflammatory and contain persistent bacteria, constituting a permissive environment for bacterial survival.
source: Because these motionless macrophages appear non-inflammatory and contain persistent bacteria, they may constitute a permissive environment for bacterial survival.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the motility and imaging data.

claim: Macrophage polarization and motility switch plays an important role in the establishment of a secure niche for Salmonella.
source: The highly dynamic changes of macrophage gene expression between early infection and persistent phases confirm the highly versatile nature of macrophage-Salmonella interactions and suggest that macrophage polarization and motility switch plays an important role in the establishment of a secure niche for Salmonella (Figure 10).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined imaging, transcriptomic, and motility data.

claim: The zebrafish larva proves to be an extraordinary platform for the analysis of Salmonella persistent infection and the understanding of long-term interactions with host cells inside a whole living animal.
source: In conclusion, the zebrafish larva proves to be an extraordinary platform for the analysis of Salmonella persistent infection and the understanding of long-term interactions with host cells inside a whole living animal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Recruited macrophages switch their phenotype from M1-like states toward non-M1 states during the time course of Salmonella infection.
source: These results reveal that recruited macrophages switch their phenotype from M1-like states toward non-M1 states during the time course of Salmonella infection and that Salmonella survives in non-M1 macrophages at late stages of infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and gene expression data showing temporal changes in macrophage phenotype.

claim: Salmonella survives in non-M1 macrophages at late stages of infection.
source: These results reveal that recruited macrophages switch their phenotype from M1-like states toward non-M1 states during the time course of Salmonella infection and that Salmonella survives in non-M1 macrophages at late stages of infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing bacterial localization in tnfa-negative macrophages at 4 dpi.

claim: In the early phase of Salmonella infection, most of the macrophages polarize toward M1 like, including both infected and bystander macrophages.
source: These results show that in the early phase of Salmonella infection, most of the macrophages polarize toward M1 like, including both infected and bystander macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data showing tnfa expression in macrophages at early time points.

claim: Both macrophages and neutrophils actively participate to the immediate innate immune response to Salmonella infection in the HBV, characterized by myelopoiesis, granulopoiesis, leukocyte recruitment to the infection site, and phagocytosis of bacteria.
source: Altogether, we concluded that both macrophages and neutrophils actively participate to the immediate innate immune response to Salmonella infection in the HBV, characterized by myelopoiesis, granulopoiesis, leukocyte recruitment to the infection site, and phagocytosis of bacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging and quantification data showing leukocyte responses.

claim: At later stages of infection, Salmonella infection triggers a massive macrophage recruitment in the HBV with formation of large macrophage clusters containing numerous persistent bacteria.
source: Altogether, these findings show that at later stages of infection, Salmonella infection triggers a massive macrophage recruitment in the HBV with formation of large macrophage clusters containing numerous persistent bacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging and quantification data at 4 dpi.

claim: Macrophages are instrumental to control Salmonella infection in HBV.
source: Altogether, these data show that macrophages are instrumental to control Salmonella infection in HBV.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the macrophage depletion experiments.

claim: Macrophages display a highly dynamic signature during the time course of infection.
source: These results reveal that macrophages display a highly dynamic signature during the time course of infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq data showing temporal changes in gene expression.

claim: Macrophages skew their phenotype from acute to persistent infection, switching from a pro-inflammatory phenotype to an anti-inflammatory/pro-regenerative phenotype with a unique cell-adhesion signature.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that macrophages skew their phenotype from acute to persistent infection, switching from a pro-inflammatory phenotype to an anti-inflammatory/pro-regenerative phenotype with a unique cell-adhesion signature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq data showing temporal changes in gene expression.

claim: The shift in adhesion program of activated macrophages during the establishment of persistent infection suggests profound changes in their interaction with their environment and their migratory properties.
source: This shift in adhesion program of activated macrophages during the establishment of persistent infection suggests profound changes in their interaction with their environment and their migratory properties.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNA-seq data showing changes in adhesion-related gene expression.

claim: During persistent infection, clusters of motionless macrophages are formed while they provide a niche for Salmonella to survive.
source: These data also demonstrate that, during persistent infection, clusters of motionless macrophages are formed while they provide a niche for Salmonella to survive.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the motility and imaging data.

claim: Cell density within tissue does not appear to affect the motility of leukocytes in persistent infection stages.
source: The observation that macrophages remained stationary while neutrophil exhibited normal mobility implies that cell density within tissue does not appear to affect the motility of leukocytes in persistent infection stages.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of macrophage and neutrophil motility.

claim: Alterations in chemokine signaling pathways may contribute to the lower motility of macrophages during persistent infection stages.
source: Chemokines also play a pivotal role in macrophage chemotaxis, and alterations in these signaling pathways may contribute to the lower motility of macrophages during persistent infection stages.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about mechanisms underlying reduced macrophage motility.

claim: The data suggest a dynamic shift in major chemotaxis signals between the acute and persistent stages of Salmonella infection that may contribute to the regulation of macrophage motility.
source: Therefore, our data suggest a dynamic shift in major chemotaxis signals between the acute and persistent stages of Salmonella infection that may contribute to the regulation of macrophage motility.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression data showing changes in chemokine expression.

claim: Salmonella persists within aggregates of tnfa-negative macrophages that remind early granulomas.
source: In the present study, Salmonella persisted within aggregates of tnfa-negative macrophages that remind early granulomas.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the imaging data comparing the observed structures to granulomas.

claim: Tnfa-negative macrophages down-regulated the expression of several tight junction-related genes during persistence, such as cdh1 and tjp1a.
source: Interestingly, in the context of persistent Salmonella infection, we showed that tnfa-negative macrophages down-regulated the expression of several tight junction-related genes during persistence, such as cdh1 and tjp1a.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing differential expression of tight junction genes.

claim: The structures observed in this study are non-epithelioid granulomas initiated by an innate immune mechanism.
source: and suggests that these structures are non-epithelioid granulomas initiated by an innate immune mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison with other granuloma types and the gene expression data.
